fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/summary: Patriarch of Alexandria (412–444) whose Christology of the one incarnate Word — Mary as Theotokos, the hypostatic union, the communication of properties — triumphed over Nestorius at Ephesus (431) and is claimed by both Chalcedonian and Oriental Orthodox churches; his ruthless politics remain controversial.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/story:
Cyril was born around 378, probably at Theodosiou in the Nile Delta, and was the nephew of Theophilus, patriarch of Alexandria, whom he accompanied to the Synod of the Oak in 403 that deposed John Chrysostom. A later Coptic tradition says he spent years among the monks of Nitria. On Theophilus’s death in 412 he was elected patriarch after rioting between factions, and quickly asserted his authority, closing the churches of the Novatianists and clashing with the imperial prefect Orestes.

The early years of his episcopate were violent. After Jewish–Christian clashes in 414–415, a large part of the Jewish community was expelled from Alexandria (the scale is debated). In March 415 the philosopher Hypatia, a respected Neoplatonist teacher and ally of Orestes, was murdered by a Christian mob led by a reader named Peter. Ancient sources such as Socrates Scholasticus blamed the climate fostered by Cyril’s party; how far Cyril himself bore responsibility is debated, but the episode has defined his modern image.

Cyril’s early theological work was exegetical and anti-Arian: commentaries on Isaiah, the Minor Prophets and John, the typological Glaphyra and On Worship in Spirit and Truth on the Pentateuch, the Thesaurus and the Dialogues on the Trinity. Later he wrote a long refutation of Julian the Apostate’s Against the Galileans, engaging Plato, Porphyry and the Hermetic writings.

In 428 Nestorius, the Antiochene-trained bishop of Constantinople, objected to calling Mary Theotokos (‘God-bearer’), preferring Christotokos. Cyril saw in this a division of Christ into two subjects that would empty the incarnation and the Eucharist of saving power. His Second Letter to Nestorius (430) and his Third Letter with twelve anathemas pressed the point; Pope Celestine supported him. At the Council of Ephesus in June 431 Cyril opened proceedings before John of Antioch and the Syrian bishops arrived and had Nestorius deposed; the Antiochenes held a rival council, and both sides lobbied the court with gifts. In 433 Cyril and John agreed the Formula of Reunion, accepting ‘a union of two natures’ and the Theotokos, and Cyril’s letter ‘Let the heavens rejoice’ (Laetentur caeli) sealed the peace.

Cyril’s favourite formula, ‘one incarnate nature (mia physis) of God the Word’, came from a text he believed to be by Athanasius but which was in fact Apollinarian. After his death in 444 both sides claimed him. The Council of Chalcedon (451) received his Second Letter to Nestorius and Laetentur caeli as standards of orthodoxy while defining Christ ‘in two natures’; the opponents of Chalcedon held that the council betrayed his ‘one nature’ formula. The Oriental Orthodox churches revere him as the ‘Pillar of Faith’, while the Chalcedonian churches read Chalcedon through his theology, especially after the Second Council of Constantinople (553).
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/roots/0/text: Athanasius’s theology of the Word who becomes flesh so that humans may become divine is the foundation of Cyril’s Christology and soteriology.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/roots/1/text: His extensive Old Testament commentaries read the Law and Prophets typologically as a shadow of Christ, in the Alexandrian tradition.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/roots/2/text: He used the school logic of his day — terms such as physis, hypostasis, ousia and idiotes and Porphyrian categories — to argue the unity of Christ.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/roots/3/text: His Against Julian engages Plato, Porphyry and the Hermetica, arguing that the best of Greek philosophy borrowed from Moses or glimpsed the Trinity dimly.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/roots/4/text: The great sees of Alexandria, Antioch, Constantinople and Rome competed for influence, and imperial favour (won partly through lavish gifts) decided councils.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/keyTeachings: The one Christ: the eternal Word is the single subject of all Christ’s acts, divine and human
Mary is Theotokos, because the one she bore is God the Word made flesh
Hypostatic union: the Word united humanity to himself ‘according to hypostasis’, not by mere indwelling or conjunction
Communication of properties: one may truly say ‘God suffered in the flesh’
The Eucharist as the life-giving flesh of the Word, the medicine of immortality
Salvation as participation in the divine nature through the Spirit and the incarnate Word
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/works/0/note: Canonised at Ephesus and Chalcedon as an authoritative statement of Christology.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/works/1/titl: Third Letter to Nestorius with the Twelve Anathemas
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/works/1/note: Uncompromising anathemas that Antiochenes regarded as Apollinarian.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/works/2/titl: Commentary on the Gospel of John
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/works/2/note: Major exegetical work written before the Nestorian controversy.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/works/3/note: Explain how the ‘one incarnate nature’ formula fits with the Formula of Reunion.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/works/4/titl: On the Unity of Christ (Quod unus sit Christus)
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/works/4/note: A late dialogue summarising his Christology.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/works/5/note: Refutation of Julian the Apostate’s Against the Galileans, preserving much of Julian’s text.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/works/6/note: Annual Paschal letters announcing the date of Easter, with doctrinal and pastoral teaching.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/doctrineCont: Defined the single-subject Christology confirmed at Ephesus (431) and normative for Chalcedonian and non-Chalcedonian churches alike.
His defence of Theotokos made Marian devotion a test of orthodoxy; the title spread in liturgy and church dedications after 431.
His theology of deification through union with the incarnate Word shaped Eastern soteriology.
Linked the Eucharist directly to the incarnation as the life-giving flesh of the Word.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/laterInfluen: His letters were canonised at Chalcedon (451); Constantinople II (553) interpreted Chalcedon in a Cyrilline sense and condemned his Antiochene opponents (the Three Chapters).
Severus of Antioch and later miaphysite theologians built on his ‘one incarnate nature’ formula; he remains the touchstone of Oriental Orthodox Christology.
Aquinas used him extensively (via the Catena aurea); Lutheran Christology, with its communicatio idiomatum, draws on Cyril.
Agreed statements between Eastern and Oriental Orthodox (1989–90) and Catholic–Coptic declarations (1973) appeal to Cyril as common ground.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/reception/0/: Venerated as the ‘Pillar of Faith’ and supreme doctor of Christology; the ‘one incarnate nature’ formula is their confession.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/reception/1/: Honoured among the great teachers; commemorated on 9 June and, with Athanasius, on 18 January.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/reception/2/: Declared Doctor of the Church by Leo XIII in 1882; feast 27 June.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/reception/3/: Rejects the Council of Ephesus and regards Cyril as the persecutor of Nestorius; recent dialogue has reduced the polemic.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/reception/4/: His Christology is accepted via the councils; his character and methods are often criticised.
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/controversie: The murder of Hypatia (415) and his responsibility for the climate of violence in Alexandria
The expulsion of Jews from Alexandria (414–415)
His conduct at Ephesus (431), opening the council before the Antiochenes arrived, and the use of gifts to win court support
The ‘one incarnate nature’ formula, derived from an Apollinarian forgery, and whether Chalcedon was faithful to him
fathers/cyril-of-alexandria/quote/text: One incarnate nature of God the Word (mia physis tou Theou Logou sesarkōmenē).
fathers/leo-the-great/summary: Pope from 440 to 461 whose Tome to Flavian supplied the Christology of the Council of Chalcedon (451) and whose sermons and letters gave classic form to the Roman doctrine of Petrine primacy.
fathers/leo-the-great/story:
Leo was probably born in Rome or Tuscany around 400 and served as a deacon under Popes Celestine I and Sixtus III, already influential enough to be consulted by John Cassian, who wrote his treatise On the Incarnation against Nestorius at Leo’s request (c. 430). He was on a diplomatic mission in Gaul when he was elected bishop of Rome in 440, and he governed the Roman church for twenty-one years — one of the longest and most consequential pontificates of late antiquity.

His lasting theological achievement was the Tome (Letter 28) sent to Flavian of Constantinople in June 449 during the Eutychian controversy. Against Eutyches’ claim that after the union Christ had only one nature, Leo set out in crisp, balanced Latin antitheses the teaching that the one person of the Word acts in each of two natures, ‘each form doing what is proper to it in communion with the other’. The Second Council of Ephesus (449) refused to read it; Leo branded that assembly a latrocinium, a ‘robber synod’. At Chalcedon in 451 the Tome was read and acclaimed — ‘Peter has spoken through Leo’ — and its language was woven into the Chalcedonian Definition.

Leo was equally the architect of a theory of the Roman see. Drawing on the language of Roman law and inheritance, he presented the pope as the ‘unworthy heir’ of Peter, in whom Peter continued to speak and to exercise a care (sollicitudo) for all the churches. He rejected Canon 28 of Chalcedon, which ranked Constantinople second to Rome on the grounds of its imperial status, insisting that Rome’s primacy rested on Peter, not on politics.

His ninety-six authentic sermons, preached on the feasts of the Roman year — Christmas, Epiphany, Lent, Easter, Pentecost and the Ember fasts — are masterpieces of Latin rhetoric with a strongly liturgical and moral bent, and some 140 letters show him disciplining bishops in Gaul and Illyricum, combating Manichaeans in Rome (443) and Priscillianists in Spain (447). Several prayers in the so-called Leonine (Verona) Sacramentary may reflect his style.

Tradition remembers him also as defender of the city: in 452 he went with a senatorial embassy to meet Attila near the Mincio and the Huns withdrew, and in 455 he persuaded the Vandal king Gaiseric to spare the population from massacre and burning during the sack of Rome. The later legend of Peter and Paul appearing over his shoulder embellishes a diplomatic success whose causes historians also find in famine and disease in Attila’s army.
fathers/leo-the-great/roots/0/text: His Christology synthesises Tertullian’s una persona, duae substantiae formula, Augustine’s anti-Pelagian sense of grace and Ambrose; Cassian’s anti-Nestorian work was written at his request.
fathers/leo-the-great/roots/1/text: His theory of the papacy borrows Roman legal categories of inheritance and office: the pope as heres of Peter, exercising a plenitudo potestatis on Peter’s behalf.
fathers/leo-the-great/roots/2/text: Trained in classical prose rhythm (the cursus), he wrote in balanced antitheses that made his Christology memorable and liturgically quotable.
fathers/leo-the-great/roots/3/text: He grounded doctrine in the Old Roman Creed and in apostolic succession at Rome, presenting the Tome as simply the baptismal faith of the Roman church.
fathers/leo-the-great/roots/4/text: He worked through emperors Theodosius II, Marcian and Valentinian III, using imperial authority to convene and enforce Chalcedon while resisting imperial ranking of sees.
fathers/leo-the-great/keyTeachings/0: One person, the eternal Word, acts in two complete natures, divine and human, each retaining its properties (communicatio idiomatum).
fathers/leo-the-great/keyTeachings/1: The Incarnation and the ‘admirable exchange’: the Son became what we are so that we might share in what he is.
fathers/leo-the-great/keyTeachings/2: Petrine primacy: Peter lives and speaks in his successors at Rome, whose care extends to the whole church.
fathers/leo-the-great/keyTeachings/3: The liturgical year as a re-presentation of the mysteries of Christ — ‘what was visible in our Redeemer has passed over into the sacraments’ (Sermon 74).
fathers/leo-the-great/keyTeachings/4: Fasting, almsgiving and prayer as the shared discipline of the Christian people.
fathers/leo-the-great/works/0/note: Classic statement of two natures in one person; read and acclaimed at Chalcedon.
fathers/leo-the-great/works/1/note: The council’s Definition draws directly on the Tome’s formulas.
fathers/leo-the-great/works/2/note: Ninety-six authentic sermons on the feasts and fasts of the Roman year.
fathers/leo-the-great/works/3/note: About 143 letters on discipline, Priscillianism, Manichaeism, Chalcedon and Canon 28.
fathers/leo-the-great/doctrineContributi: The Tome supplied the Latin, two-nature language of Chalcedon and remains the West’s classic statement of Christ’s person.
Gave enduring form to the doctrine of Roman primacy grounded in Peter rather than in imperial status.
His sermons interpret the feasts as present participations in the saving mysteries, shaping Roman liturgical theology.
fathers/leo-the-great/laterInfluence/0/t: Gregory the Great and Gelasius I built on his theory of Petrine office; Maximus the Confessor defended the Tome against Monothelites.
fathers/leo-the-great/laterInfluence/1/t: Medieval canonists and Gregory VII inherited his legal vocabulary of plenitude of power and Petrine heirship.
fathers/leo-the-great/laterInfluence/2/t: Luther and Calvin respected his Christology but read his Petrine theology as a decisive step toward papal monarchy.
fathers/leo-the-great/laterInfluence/3/t: Twentieth-century Orthodox–Oriental Orthodox dialogues (1989–90) examined whether the Tome and Cyril’s miaphysite language are compatible.
fathers/leo-the-great/reception/0/text: Venerated as saint and declared a Doctor of the Church by Benedict XIV in 1754; feast 10 November.
fathers/leo-the-great/reception/1/text: Honoured as an Orthodox saint and defender of Chalcedon (feast 18 February), though his papal theology is not accepted.
fathers/leo-the-great/reception/2/text: Coptic, Syriac and Armenian churches historically rejected the Tome as Nestorianising and anathematised it; recent dialogue has softened but not erased this.
fathers/leo-the-great/reception/3/text: Valued as a witness to Chalcedonian orthodoxy and an outstanding preacher, while his claims for Rome are rejected.
fathers/leo-the-great/controversies/0: The Tome’s dyophysite language was rejected by Dioscorus and the non-Chalcedonian churches, contributing to the lasting schism after 451.
fathers/leo-the-great/controversies/1: His refusal of Canon 28 of Chalcedon foreshadowed later Rome–Constantinople rivalry.
fathers/leo-the-great/controversies/2: His use of imperial power against Manichaeans and Priscillianists raises questions about coercion in religious matters.
fathers/leo-the-great/quote/text: Christian, acknowledge your dignity; having been made a partner in the divine nature, do not return to your former baseness.
fathers/leo-the-great/places/3/name: Near Mantua, on the Mincio (meeting with Attila)
